UNITED NATIONS
 DEVELOPMENT
 ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK
 (2002-2006)
 ERITREA
 May 2002ForewordForeword 
Since Eritrea's emergence as a sovereign state following a UN-supervised referendum in 1993, the
United Nations has been a close partner of the newly-independent country. This began with the
Reconstruction and Rehabilitation phase that spanned the early years of independence and the
development cooperation stage when the various UN agencies had their first country programmes in
full swing. Significant results were achieved in the years 1992 - 1997, particularly in the area of
expanding access to basic social services - namely elementary education and primary health care, as
well as rehabilitation, expansion and improvement of basic rural infrastructures. The progressively
improving social and economic indicators evidenced by the increasingly enhanced Human
Development standing of Eritrea are an indication of this progress. This is a success that the UN
family in Eritrea is proud to be part of.
The border conflict that broke out between Eritrea and Ethiopia in May 1998 was an unfortunate
development that had dramatic effects not only on the programmes of cooperation of the UN, but,
most regrettably, on the entire population, the economy and people's livelihoods. In the humanitarian 
relief efforts to alleviate the human suffering that resulted, and in the subsequent recovery phase that 
followed the signing of the Peace Agreement in December 2000, the UN joined hands with other
partners to support the government's herculean task of responding to the vast humanitarian and
recovery needs.
It was at the height of this humanitarian emergency, in the year 2000, that the UN Country Team,
together with Government, donor and civil society partners, embarked on the process of carrying out 
the Common Country Assessment (CCA). This highly collaborative process was followed by the
formulation phase of the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF), which has
culminated in the current document. Here we can see how, for the first time in Eritrea, the UN
System collectively articulates its response, in a coherent manner, to the development and recovery
priorities of the country. By addressing national priorities in those areas where it could best make a
difference, the UN System also takes inspiration from the Millennium Development Goals (MDGS)
to which the whole of humanity, as represented by its governments and civil society, has committed
itself. As part of upholding the spirit of UN Reform at the country level and responding to the
government's own preferences, the UN System will increasingly make proactive efforts to implement 
the UNDAF through joint programmes.
The launching of the first UNDAF for Eritrea also comes at an opportune moment, in two respects. 
Firstly, it follows the verdict of the Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission, which, by virtue of
having been accepted by both governments, signals the dawn of a lasting peace. It also comes at a
time when recovery activities are already well underway, paving the way for a full resumption of
regular development endeavours.

UN Development Assistance Framework for Eritrea 
2002 – 2006 
We aim to better life for all Eritreans, especially the poor and those affected by war and drought, by
supporting the socioeconomic development objectives of the State of Eritrea through a unified,
comprehensive and coherent partnership. By upholding the above-mentioned goals we aim to build
sustainable livelihoods, foster peace and good governance, and achieve post-conflict recovery.
In pursuing these goals, we will undertake joint/collaborative programmes, common monitoring and
evaluation, and ensure transparent and accountable use of resources. We shall encourage the
development of civil society, the empowerment of local authorities and communities, and promote the 
rights of women, men and children. Through the collective efforts of the Government, UN and other 
partners, a basis will be laid for sustainable human development in Eritrea.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The UNDAF for Eritrea aims to contribute to the achievement of the overarching goals laid out in the United
Nations Millennium Declaration resulting from the September 2000 General Assembly Summit of the heads of
state and Government. These goals include halving the proportion of people living in extreme poverty, suffering 
from hunger, and without access to safe water; enrolling all children in primary school and eliminating gender
disparity in primary and secondary education; reducing maternal, infant, and under-five mortality rates; halting
and beginning to reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS; providing access for all to reproductive health services; and
implementing national strategies for sustainable development to reverse the loss of environmental resources.
In pursuing these goals, UN agencies will undertake joint programmes, common monitoring and evaluation, and 
ensure transparent and accountable use of resources. They shall encourage the development of civil society, the
empowerment of local authorities and communities, and promote the rights of women, men and children.
Through the collective efforts of the Government, UN and NGO community, a basis will be laid for sustainable 
human development in Eritrea. 
THE DEVELOPMENT SITUATION
Eritrea has a resident population of over 3 million and land area of 125,700 sq. km. The per capita GDP was
estimated to be around US$ 2001 (US$880 PPP2) in 1998. In terms of UNDP’s human development index, it
ranked 148th out of 162 countries included in UNDP’s Human Development Report of 2001. 
Eritrea became formally independent following an internationally supervised referendum in April 1993 - two
years after the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front achieved a decisive military victory over Ethiopia in May
1991. Until the start of the border conflict with Ethiopia in May 1998, the new government had pursued policies, 
strategies and investments to promote rapid and equitable economic growth led by the private sector. By early
1998, most of the transition issues had been addressed, investor confidence was beginning to grow, private
investment in a number of sectors was increasing and the economy was growing rapidly.
Unfortunately, Eritrea’s initial promising growth was disrupted by the border conflict with Ethiopia that started
in May 1998 and resulted in a war that continued until June 2000. The war has not only caused loss of human
life, displacement of nearly one-third of the total population (about one million people), and huge damage to
physical infrastructure, but has also reversed the positive economic trends of the pre-conflict post independence 
period. In addition to its devastating social and human impact, the conflict has resulted in:
• a decline in real GDP growth from about 8% (1993-1997) to 3.9 percent in 1998, 0.8 percent in 1999, 
and a negative growth of 8.2 percent in 2000;
• inflation soaring from an average of 6 percent during 1994-97 to 27 percent in 2000;
• international reserves falling from 5 months of imports to less than one month in 2000; and
• fiscal deficit rising from 6 percent of GDP in 1997 to 48 percent of GDP in 2000.
At present, the country faces two daunting development challenges. Firstly, meeting immediate needs for
emergency humanitarian assistance, reconstructing infrastructure damaged during the war, assisting nearly onethird of the displaced population resume their economic activities, demobilizing and reintegrating nearly 
200,000 soldiers mobilized for the war effort, reintegrating returning refugees, rebuilding the economy,
restoring social services and completing the economic and political reforms initiated before the conflict began.
Secondly, begin to plan a medium-to-long-term development programme to attain rapid, sustainable, pro-poor 
economic growth and reduction of poverty in an environmentally sound manner, led by a dynamic private sector

GOVERNMENT DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY AND PRIORITIES
The Government’s Transitional Economic Development and Poverty Reduction Strategy of September 2001 has 
identified its development assistance priorities in terms of two distinct time frames. The government’s
immediate priorities, covering 2001-2002, are to rebuild the economy, restore social services and complete the
economic and political reforms initiated before the conflict began. For the medium term (2003-2005), 
government’s overarching objectives are to attain rapid, sustainable, widely shared economic growth and
reduction of poverty in an environmentally sound manner, led by a dynamic private sector.
Specifically, the government’s priorities over the next two years or so are to focus on: (i) meeting immediate
needs for emergency humanitarian assistance; (ii) reconstructing infrastructure, assisting displaced people
resume their economic activities, and reintegrating Eritrean refugees returning to the country; (iii) restoring a
stable and supportive fiscal and macroeconomic framework; and (iv) demobilizing soldiers and reintegrating
them into the economy. Addressing these immediate challenges is key to continuing previously initiated critical 
development projects.
Over the medium term (2003-05), the government’s development priorities include:
• Developing new export markets. 
• Rebuilding the port business.
• Increasing agricultural productivity. 
• Achieving macroeconomic stability. 
• Attracting private sector investment. 
• Privatizing government-owned enterprises.
• Developing a sound financial system. 
The strategy document has identified the following three areas of special emphasis in Eritrea’s current economic 
development programme, which are also referred to as cross-sectoral priorities:
• Demobilizing and reintegrating soldiers.
• Enhancing the status and increasing the participation of women in development.
• Restoring, enhancing, and preserving Eritrea’s ecological integrity.
UN SYSTEM’S STRATEGY FOR MEETING THE DEVELOPMENT CHALLENGES IN ERITREA
The UN system’s strategy for meeting the development challenges of Eritrea is to deliver its assistance on two
parallel tracks. One focuses on supporting national efforts to respond to the country’s immediate needs for relief 
and recovery. At the same time, on a parallel track, the UN system will support the government in the planning
and implementation of its medium-to-long-term development programme as outlined above. 
To ensure that the activities undertaken during the emergency/transition phase are compatible and consistent
with the medium-to-long-term development goals, the UN system will provide support for strengthening the
needed coordination mechanisms involving the relevant government departments, the UN system agencies, and
other development partners. As part of the UNDAF process, the UN system agencies in Eritrea are committed to 
coordinating their programming activities more closely. 
In response to the country’s immediate emergency humanitarian assistance needs, the UN system, in
collaboration with the government, has devised programmes and the required resources for the year 2002 are
currently being mobilized through a Consolidated Appeal Process (CAP). The target is to mobilize around US $ 
120.5 million of grant resources. The activities that are planned to be financed through these resources includeiii
UNDAF Eritrea, 2002 - 2006
both emergency/relief activities, such as food aid as well as rehabilitation, reintegration and reconstruction
activities that have implications for the medium-to-long term development goals. In subsequent years,
availability of resources, through the CAP, will depend on the nature and magnitude of emergencies that may
lapse or arise. 
In addition to emergency humanitarian assistance, the UN system’s grant assistance earmarked for supporting
multi-year programmes that are part of the approved country programmes is estimated at around US $ 119.6
million for the 2002-2006 period. The UN agencies will continue to work with the government to mobilize
additional resources to provide humanitarian assistance and for activities where they have a comparative
advantage.
The goal of the UN Country Team in Eritrea is to contribute towards fostering peace and good governance,
achieving post-conflict recovery, strengthening of basic social services, building sustainable livelihoods and
stimulating equitable economic growth to promote the achievement of the overarching goal of poverty
reduction. The UN Country Team in Eritrea, in close consultation with the Government and key stakeholders,
has agreed upon three key strategic objectives for UN System support under the first UNDAF for Eritrea:
ß Promotion of Democratic Governance.
ß Promotion of Access to Quality Basic Social Services.
ß Promotion of Pro-Poor Economic Growth and Sustainable Livelihoods.
To promote democratic governance, the UN system in Eritrea will support: the development of a justice system 
that fosters the rule of law and social justice; the development and strengthening of participatory decentralized 
institutions; development of an effective, efficient, transparent and accountable civil service; facilitating
participation of civil society organizations in national development processes; and advocacy for the ratification 
of global conventions.
To promote access to quality basic social services, the UN system agencies will support: the development of an 
education and training system that can meet the national needs and the global goal of equitable quality primary
education for all by 2015; work towards improving the nutritional status of the population, especially women
and children; Government programmes on early childhood development and initiatives aimed at ensuring that
all individuals and families have access to fully integrated quality health services, including reproductive health, 
through governmental and non-governmental facilities and community health services; and Government efforts
to provide all citizens with access to shelter, safe and adequate water, sanitation and a hygienic environment. 
Halting and beginning to reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS is one of the millennium goals for international
development assistance (United Nations Millennium Declaration, September 2000). Furthermore, in June 2001,
the United Nations General Assembly Special Session on HIV/AIDS declared HIV/AIDS a global emergency
and one of the most formidable challenges to human life and dignity. At present, Eritrea is in a fortunate
position of having a low prevalence rate and a strong political commitment to controlling the epidemic. Under
the first UNDAF for Eritrea, the UN system agencies will support the promotion of a strong multi-sectoral 
national response to HIV/AIDS and other key diseases.
To promote pro-poor economic growth and sustainable livelihoods, the UN system’s assistance will be focused 
on: support for government initiatives and programmes to achieve pro-poor economic growth; reducing food
insecurity to alleviate poverty; support for sustainable management of the environment, natural resources and
energy; expanded access to telecommunications and internet services; and support for the collection, analysis,
and dissemination of data needed for development planning, including a comprehensive poverty assessment. 
Building on existing coordination mechanisms, particularly those established in the CCA process, the following 
structures will be used for the coordination, monitoring and review of UNDAF implementation:iv

UNDAF Steering Committee: The existing UNDAF Steering Committee, consisting of UN Heads of
Agencies, Macro Policy and the Ministry of Local Government, will be maintained to provide policy level
oversight to the implementation, monitoring and review of the UNDAF. The expanded version of the
Steering Committee will include, in addition to the above, Government and UN co-chairs of the Thematic
Groups and Sub-groups. Terms of reference of the Steering Committee as well as those of the Thematic
Groups appear under Annex VI.
Thematic Groups: To bring greater coherence to UN agencies’ programmes, a number of thematic groups 
and sub-groups will be established. These groups will be responsible for: (a) ensuring that inter-agency joint 
programming opportunities are maximized; (b) coordinating UN agencies’ programme activities in the
focus area of the thematic group; (c) coordination between UN system agencies and relevant government
ministries/agencies; and (d) joint monitoring, reviews and evaluation of activities. Four theme groups, and
six sub-groups will continue to provide theme-focused follow up to UNDAF implementation3. These are: I. 
Basic Social Services, under which there are four sub-groups, namely: (i) Health and Nutrition (ii)
Education (iii) Water and Sanitation, and (iv) HIV/AIDS; II. Sustainable Livelihoods and Pro-poor 
Economic Growth, with (i) Poverty Reduction (ii) Food Security as sub-groups; III. Recovery; and IV. 
Data for Development. Detailed description of these groups is provided in Annex V. 
Common Database for Monitoring UNDAF Implementation: An on-line computerized database will be
developed to maintain up-to-date statistics related to the indicators for monitoring UNDAF implementation 
as specified in Annex VII. The National Statistics and Evaluation Office (NSEO) will have the primary
responsibility for maintaining this on-line system with support from the UN Resident Coordination Office.
It will be supported by designated staff in the relevant Government and UN agencies who will be
responsible for updating parts of the system relevant to their mandates.

INTRODUCTION
1.1 MISSION OF THE UN SYSTEM IN 
ERITREA
1. The UNDAF for Eritrea aims to
contribute to the achievement of the
overarching goals laid out in the United
Nations Millennium Declaration resulting
from the September 2000 General
Assembly Summit of the heads of state and government. These goals include halving the proportion
of people living in extreme poverty, suffering from hunger, and without access to safe water; enrolling 
all children in primary school and eliminating gender disparity in primary and secondary education; 
reducing maternal, infant, and under-five mortality rates; halting and beginning to reverse the spread 
of HIV/AIDS; providing access for all to reproductive health services; and implementing national
strategies for sustainable development to reverse the loss of environmental resources.
2. Within this framework, the UN Country Team in Eritrea aims to better life for all Eritreans,
especially the poor and those affected by war and drought, by supporting the socio-economic 
development objectives of the State of Eritrea through a unified, comprehensive and coherent
partnership. By upholding the above-mentioned goals it aims to build sustainable livelihoods, foster
peace and good governance, and achieve post-conflict recovery. 
3. In pursuing these goals, UN agencies will undertake joint/collaborative programmes, common
monitoring and evaluation, and ensure transparent and accountable use of resources. They shall
encourage the development of civil society, the empowerment of local authorities and communities,
and promote the equal rights of women, men and children. Through the collective efforts of the
Government, UN and NGO community, a basis will be laid for sustainable human development in
Eritrea. 
1.2 THE PURPOSE AND OBJECTIVES OF UNDAF
4. In 1997, the Secretary-General of the United Nations launched a programme of reform for the
United Nations with the aim of preparing it for the challenges of the 21st century. A number of the
reform actions set forth by the Secretary-General address the development work of the United
Nations, a core mission that remains of vital importance. One of the key elements of this reform is to 
bring greater coherence to United Nations programmes of assistance at the country level with
common objectives and time frames in close consultation with governments. The United Nations
Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for a country is the instrument that has been designed 
to achieve this element of the UN reform programme.
5. The UNDAF is the planning framework for the development operations of the UN system at
country level. It lays the foundation for cooperation among the UN system agencies, government and 
other development partners through the preparation of a complementary set of programmes and
projects. As a consequence, it enables the UN system to achieve “goal-oriented collaboration,
coherence and mutual reinforcement” called for by the UN Secretary-General and endorsed by the UN 
General Assembly in resolution 53/192.
6. The UNDAF aims for greater impact of UN System cooperation on the development and
well being of the people through:2
UNDAF Eritrea, 2002 - 2006
• improved focus and result orientation, identifying where the UN system can make the most
difference using its unique strengths as a development partner;
• stronger unity of purpose and team spirit within the UN system;
• increased collaboration through a mix of agency, parallel and joint programming;
• better integration of the normative and operational aspects of development cooperation;
• increased dialogue and stronger partnerships and alliances with other members of the
development community such as national and global civil society, the private sector, bilateral 
donors, the World Bank and other international financial institutions (IFIs), and the European 
Commission;
• more efficient use of limited resources, based on improved division of labor, rationalization of 
resource allocation and streamlining of procedures; and
• improved opportunities for securing increased resources in support of national needs and
priorities.
7. The UNDAF serves as the common frame of reference for the strategy and country programme 
documents (or other similar instruments) as well as any joint programme documents, used by
participating UN system organizations for development cooperation at country level.
1.3 THE UNDAF PREPARATION PROCESS
8. Work on the preparation of the first UNDAF for Eritrea began in April 2000 when the UN
country team in Eritrea embarked on the task of preparing the first Common Country Assessment
(CCA) for Eritrea. The CCA for Eritrea, completed in March 2001 under very difficult conditions,
was a country-based process that reviewed and analyzed the national development situation and
identified key development issues. This process, launched by the UN Resident Coordinator, involved 
the active participation of senior government officials, representatives of civil society organizations,
private sector and bilateral/multilateral agencies present in Eritrea. They participated in the
preparation of analyses in eight thematic areas. The selection of the thematic areas to be assessed and 
analyzed by the Theme Groups was based primarily on the areas of focus agreed upon by the UN and 
Government of the State of Eritrea in the Country Strategy Note (CSN) in 1998. They were also
selected by virtue of their significant contribution to poverty reduction and promotion of human
development, which constitute the over-arching objectives of the UN in Eritrea. The eight thematic
areas were: (i) Governance; (ii) Economic growth and development; (iii) Food security; (iv)
Education; (v) Health; (vi) Shelter/water and sanitation; (vii) Environment and energy; and (viii)
Emergency recovery, reintegration and rehabilitation. In addition, eight issues that are linked with
several thematic areas were analyzed. These included: (i) HIV/AIDS & STDs; (ii) nutrition; (iii)
gender in development; (vi) capacity development; (v) issues of equity; (vi) communication for
development; (vii) population groups with special needs; and (viii) data for development.
9. The process of UNDAF preparation was managed by a “Steering Committee”, composed of
Heads of UN Agencies and senior government officials. It provided overall leadership and guidance
to the UNDAF preparation process. The Steering Committee was supported by three “Theme Groups” 
who were responsible for developing the logical framework for the areas identified by the Steering
Committee as priority areas for UN System support. The three thematic groups, representing the three 
Strategic Objectives of the UNDAF, were in turn supported by a number of sub-groups who focused 
on specific priority areas. 3

2.1 THE DEVELOPMENT SITUATION
11. Eritrea has a resident population of
over 3 million and occupies a land area of 
125,700 square kilometers. The per capita
GDP was estimated to be around US$ 200 
(US$880 PPP4) in 1998. In terms of
UNDP’s human development index, it ranked 148th out of 162 countries included in UNDP’s Human 
Development Report of 2001. 
12. Eritrea became formally independent following an internationally supervised referendum in
April 1993, two years after the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front achieved a decisive military victory 
over Ethiopia in May 1991. Successive colonial administrations and neglect lasting over a century, a
protracted war of liberation lasting over three decades, and intermittent droughts severely damaged
Eritrea’s infrastructure, development institutions and productive capacity. Consequently, at the time
of liberation, devastated infrastructure, weak institutions, and technologically backward agricultural,
manufacturing and service sectors characterized the country’s economy. 
13. In the post independence period, the Government of Eritrea adopted a two-pronged approach to 
tackle its development challenges. Firstly, by addressing the immediate challenges of resuscitating the 
economy and rehabilitating key sectors through promoting an outward-oriented, private-sector-led 
market economy. Secondly, by looking beyond the horizon of immediate problems and examining in
depth the long-term prospects to devise an appropriate macro framework and supporting policies. It
also moved away decisively from the central planning system it had inherited.
14. Until the start of the border conflict with Ethiopia in May 1998, the new government had
pursued policies, strategies and investments to promote rapid and equitable economic growth led by
the private sector. It embarked on creating an enabling policy environment and investing in
infrastructure and strategic industries. It adopted an investment code that opened up the economy to
private investors, and began to rehabilitate, upgrade and expand transportation, communications,
power, and water supply facilities; improved the capacity of the health care, education, and financial 
systems to deliver services; and restored the productive capacity of the economy particularly in
agriculture and fisheries, tourism, construction, mining and manufacturing. These policies resulted in 
significant progress in education and health care during the 1992-97 period. School enrollment
increased and there was a sharp decline in infant and child mortality rates. Eritrea’s real GDP grew at 
an average annual rate of seven percent during this period. By early 1998, most of the transition

15. Unfortunately, Eritrea’s initial promising growth was disrupted by the border conflict with
Ethiopia that started in May 1998 and subsequently escalated into full-scale war in the ensuing two
years. This unnecessary war has not only caused loss of human life, displacement of nearly one-third 
of the population (about one million people), and huge damage to physical infrastructure, but also
reversed the positive economic trends of the pre-conflict, post independence period. The country’s
food security situation has also been adversely affected by persistent drought over the last three years. 
Mobilization of the population between the ages of 18 to 40 for the war effort has resulted in critical 
shortages of professional, skilled, and semi-skilled workers in both the public and private sectors,
adversely affecting the delivery of public sector services, agricultural output, and the productive
capacity of the private sector. In addition to its devastating social and human impact, the conflict has 
resulted in:
• a decline in real GDP growth from about 8% (1993-1997) to 3.9 percent in 1998, 0.8 percent 
in 1999, and a negative growth of 8.2 percent in 2000;
• inflation soaring from an average of 6 percent during 1994-97 to 27 percent in 2000;
• international reserves falling from 5 months of imports to less than one month in 2000; and
• fiscal deficit rising from 6 percent of GDP in 1997 to 48 percent of GDP in 2000.
16. At present, the country faces two daunting development challenges. Firstly, meeting immediate 
needs for emergency humanitarian assistance, reconstructing infrastructure damaged during the war,
assisting nearly one-third of the displaced population to resume their economic activities,
demobilizing and reintegrating nearly 200,000 combatants mobilized for the war effort, rebuilding the 
economy, restoring social services and completing the economic and political reforms initiated before 
the conflict began. Secondly, planning a medium to long-term development programme to attain
rapid, sustainable, pro-poor economic growth and reduction of poverty in an environmentally sound
manner, led by a dynamic private sector based on the founding principles of Eritrea’s constitution:
participatory development, equitable economic growth, social justice, and the rule of law.
17. Although data on poverty is extremely limited, proxy indicators would suggest a relatively high 
level of overall poverty when defined to include income as well as access to and utilization of public 
services. A rapid appraisal undertaken in 1993/94 estimated that 69% of the population of Eritrea
were living in poverty. The highest concentration of the poor was found in the highlands followed by 
the urban areas. 
18. The recent war with Ethiopia (1998-2000) has directly affected the livelihoods of more than 1
million people who were forced to flee from the advancing Ethiopian army. The war created
numerous female-headed households and orphans and has placed an additional burden on women and 
children. Another poverty inducing impact of the war and drought has been an increase in prices of
basic commodities, including foodstuffs, making it more difficult for many families to afford a well
balanced diet. Limited access to social and economic services has also perpetuated poverty and
reduced the overall capacity of the country to develop.6
UNDAF Eritrea, 2002 - 2006
19. In Eritrea, livelihoods are vulnerable to climatic conditions and environmental degradation. The 
depletion of forests, woodlands and water resources has indirectly affected the children’s schooling,
especially girls’ education, as domestic responsibilities become cumbersome and time consuming.
20. In rural areas, up to 97 percent of the energy consumption is derived from biomass sources.
Fuel-wood collection and charcoal-making aggravate deforestation, and diversion of cow dung and
crop residue for fuel deprives the soil of organic nutrients, thus depressing productivity.
21. Eritrea lies in a semi-arid zone, and has low and unreliable rainfall and, except for the Setit, the 
country has no perennial river. The full extent of the country’s water resources (ground and
underground) is not known. At present, available water resources are scarce. At the same time, the
rich marine resources of the Eritrean Red Sea are not optimally utilized.
22. Eritrea has had a persistent food deficit. Agricultural production is adversely affected by low
productivity due to poor technology and land tenure practices, high losses of crops and livestock due 
to pests, continuous degradation of the soil, forest and water bodies, extreme rainfall variability with 
recurrent and long drought periods, inadequacy in processing and marketing systems, and lack of
research and extension services. Land is almost the sole source of income for more than 80 percent of 
the Eritrean population and its degradation is a serious problem. So far soil and water conservation on 
farmland has not received adequate attention. It is estimated that roughly 16 percent of the total land 
area is arable – of which only about a quarter is actually cultivated. 
23. During the long period of struggle for liberation, provision of formal education had severely
suffered. After independence, Eritrea faced the daunting task of putting in place an education and
training infrastructure almost from scratch. Although significant progress has been made, the task of
establishing an education and training system that can meet its development needs remains a
challenge. 
24. Although civil society organizations could have built on a pre-independence tradition, so far
they are only a few in number and not well developed. Since independence, substantial efforts have
been made to promote private-sector-led economic development. While it is a matter of policy that the 
State should undertake only what the private sector cannot do, the State is still an important player in 
strategic sectors of the country’s economy. At the same time, public sector institutions suffer from
severe capacity gaps. Many ministries lack modern planning tools and data. In the immediate postindependence period, PFDJ’s5
 fully or partially owned enterprises have made a valuable contribution
in uplifting the devastated economy that it inherited at independence. To achieve a broad based private 
sector growth that is essential for achieving sustained economic growth and the government’s
economic growth targets, a pre-requisite now is the creation of an enabling environment that is
perceived by potential entrepreneurs to be fair and transparent. An important step in this direction
would be to provide, periodically, financial information on the economic operations of the PFDJ. 
25. There is a huge need for investment in information technology. Dramatic changes in
technology must be accompanied by serious reorganization of the way that business is undertaken in
order to reap the full benefit of interventions.

26. Notwithstanding the added challenges resulting from the recent war, the most critical
constraints that continue to affect Eritrea’s socio-economic development include:
Human resource deficiency: This has been the greatest bottleneck in Eritrea’s development efforts. In 
the short-term the Government is tackling the problem by importing foreign experts on a temporary
basis and as a long-term strategy through a concerted national effort aimed at increasing educational
and skill development opportunities.
A financial and foreign exchange gap: With a low per capita income and widespread poverty,
Eritrea’s ability to mobilize sufficient domestic savings to finance domestic investments is limited.
Physical infrastructure: The extent and quality of Eritrea’s infrastructure are still inadequate to attract 
private investment. 
Institutional capacity: Though much has been done to improve Eritrea’s administrative, legal,
commercial, judiciary and regulatory institutions, much remains to be done to achieve a standard that 
fosters investor confidence and private sector participation in long term investments. 
Inadequate data: Although improvements have been made over the last eight years, there is still a lack 
of relevant, timely and reliable economic and social data. There is no reasonably accurate data on
national income, fiscal and monetary developments, price indices, and demographic and social trends. 
27. After 30 years of struggle for independence and the recent war, Eritrean society is faced with
the challenge of rebuilding and developing not only its physical and economic infrastructure, but also 
its human potential. The development of human potential requires the creation of an environment in
which all can enjoy long, healthy and creative lives through equal access to, and participation in, the 
economic, social, and cultural life of the nation. 
28. Despite the challenging scenario presented above, a number of enabling factors to achieve
development goals are also currently present. The most important prerequisite for these factors to be
effective, however, is an environment of peace and tranquility. One important element of the peace 
dividend is a greater availability of resources for development. A successful reprioritization of public 
sector expenditures can make a swift return to pre-war levels a reality. 
29. A second factor is that more partners and resources are now available in country to support
the development process. The current and planned interventions of the World Bank, UN system, and 
bilateral donors have the potential to make a major impact. In addition, several international NGO’s
are present and have signaled their desire to stay for the longer term. Major donors in country include 
the Italian Cooperation, USAID, DANIDA, SIDA, the Netherlands, the European Union, Norway and 
others. In addition, several embassies support trade and investment initiatives as well as projects
relevant to human development including construction of social amenities, training and provision of
basic inputs. 
30. The third factor is the relatively un-exploited natural resource base including marine 
resources, arable land of which only a small proportion is currently being used and minerals. If peace 
prevails one could also reasonably expect an influx of foreign investment and opportunities for
increased tourism. Finally the human resource potential of Eritrea is significant and investments in
human capital are likely to yield high returns for human development. In addition, Eritreans abroad
form a pool of highly trained and skilled professionals whose expertise could and should be enlisted
for national development.8

2.2 MAJOR ACHIEVEMENTS
31. Governance: Within the context of a number of international human rights instruments,
Governance may be defined, among other things, as the exercise of economic, political and
administrative authority to manage a country's affairs at all levels, comprising the mechanisms,
processes, and institutions through which authority is directed. This authority is circumscribed by a
system of fundamental human rights, freedoms and duties that in the case of Eritrea are enshrined in 
the Constitution, ratified on 23 May 1997 by the National Assembly. 
32. The Government’s major achievements to-date include: the 1992 referendum that led to the
establishment of an independent state; the ratification of the Constitution in 1997 by an elected body; 
the proclamation of laws amending the Ethiopian codes; the 1997 Ministry of Justice programme to
upgrade the legal system; local and regional Baito elections; the public sector management review;
and the 1996 Decentralization Proclamation. Eritrea has also ratified various international human
rights conventions and has signed the Geneva Conventions. The Ministry of Justice is in the process
of identifying additional measures to ensure that these rights are fully respected. Decentralization and 
devolution of power has been pursued for less than four years (1997-2000). While some achievements 
can be noted for Debub and Gash Barka regions before the recent conflict, in general, human resource 
and material limitations have persisted.
33. The practice of democratic election has a long history in Eritrea. Local elections have always 
been organised at village level and the practice continued during the struggle for independence.
Though the development of an electoral law has been hampered by the recent conflict with Ethiopia, 
since the signing of the Peace Agreement in December 2000, two important laws have been drafted:
one dealing with the electoral system and the other with the setting up of political parties. The draft
law to govern the formation and conduct of political parties is now under public debate.

36. Real progress was made in all sectors of

37. Unfortunately, Eritrea’s initial

heightened mobilization of men and women,

primarily because of the fall in agricultural output. In all, the loss of output, measured as the
difference between the pre-conflict trend growth rate and actual output, totals about US$380 million.
38. Food security: The most fundamental right to adequate living standards, including food, is
contained in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The World Food Summit set the goal of
halving malnutrition by 2015. Eritrea is among the countries with the highest food insecurity and
malnutrition. The food security situation has been further aggravated by the recent border conflict. 
39. The areas most affected by the war, Gash-Barka and Debub, are also the nation’s most
agriculturally productive, accounting for about 70 percent of total grain output. The fighting and
widespread displacement prevented farmers from planting crops. Grain output in the country fell
from a total of 460,000 metric tons in 1998 to 320,000 metric tons in 1999 and to 85,000 metric tons 
in 2000. This has exacerbated an already critical food shortage arising from the drought. While 
output should be higher during 2001 because many farmers have been able to return to their farms,
about 1.8 million citizens - nearly half of Eritrea’s population - will require food assistance during the 
coming 12–18 months.10

40. Education: The Dakar Framework for Action on Education for All (EFA) has identified the
expansion and improvement of early childhood care and education to guarantee free, compulsory and 
good quality education to all children by 2015, and to achieve 50% improvement in levels of adult
literacy by 2015, especially for women. The Government of Eritrea strives for equal opportunity for
disadvantaged groups, capacity development at all levels in the education system, the elimination of
disparities in primary and secondary education, systematic quality control, and the strengthening of
vocational technical education and educational infrastructure.
41. An important milestone in the Eritrean struggle for independence has been the development of a 
new Eritrean education system. Education, during the struggle, was seen as part of the liberating
process. Attempts were made to reach all citizens irrespective of their gender, ethnicity, religion,
location and occupation (including nomads) through formal and non-formal means. Education as a
fundamental right of the child is enshrined in the Eritrean Constitution and emphasized in the Macro 
Policy and the National Economic Policy Framework.
42. The ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and the Convention on the 
Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) are expressions of the
national commitment to implementation of the educational right of the child. The education policy
focuses on the eradication of illiteracy. It calls for the provision of free and compulsory basic
education (5 years of primary plus 2 years of middle level); the use of the mother tongue teaching at
the primary level; and the expansion of secondary and tertiary education opportunities as essential
components. In addition to basic education there is a special need to cater for the requirements of an 
expanding private sector-led economy and to give special emphasis to technical and business subjects 
in higher learning institutions.
43. Within the limits of available resources since independence, significant progress has been made 
in the provision of education services. In the post independence era, development of education and
training systems in Eritrea has been focused on filling critical gaps. There is ample evidence that
significant progress has been made over the last decade. A national EFA Framework of Action has
been drafted in a process that involved extensive national dialogue on EFA as a basis for the longterm vision of education in Eritrea. To ensure systematic development of the education and training
systems there is now an urgent need to develop a comprehensive development plan for the education 
and training systems to meet the needs of a growing economy, and more importantly, to enable
citizens to acquire skills to effectively participate in the productive activities of the nation. The plan
should ensure not only integrated development of all levels of the formal education and training
systems but must also ensure that developments in education and training systems are closely linked
with the demands of a growing labor market.
44. Health and Nutrition: The international goals set for 2015 include universal access to primary
and reproductive health services and information by 2015, reduction of the infant mortality rate by 1/3 
of 1990 level and below 35 per 1000, reduction of the child mortality rate by 2/3, improved maternal 
health and reduced maternal mortality by one half based on 2000 levels. In order to ensure the best
possible health status for all Eritreans within a resource-constrained environment, the Ministry of
Health is following a Primary Health Care approach. This means a focus on health promotion, and
prevention of illness as the first line of action, linked with the provision of affordable basic health
services in the periphery, and a viable referral mechanism between different levels of care. 11
UNDAF Eritrea, 2002 - 2006
45. Presently, all calculations on health statistics are based on the 1995 Eritrean Demographic and
Health Survey (EDHS) and population estimates from the Zones. The State of Eritrean Management
Information System for Health (SEMISH) is fully operational but only captures health institutionbased data. Activities in the community such as deliveries are not captured. Discrepancies between
the data collected by SEMISH and the data collected, through various mechanisms have been
observed including calculations and target age groups on immunization, nutrition, and HIV/AIDS.
This needs to be synchronized. A second Demographic and Health Survey planned for 2002 will help 
to establish a better understanding of the current situation.
46. While the health status of Eritreans remains poor, the Government of Eritrea has already
achieved major improvements. Since independence, the number of health facilities has significantly
increased, existing health centers have been rehabilitated, the number of health workers has increased, 
a domestic drug manufacturing capacity has been established, and significant improvements have
been achieved in the distribution of oral rehydration sachets, and immunization of 1 year olds against 
key childhood illnesses including measles, polio, tuberculosis etc..
47. Water, shelter and sanitation: Water and Sanitation for all by 2015 was set as a target by the
Earth Summit in 1992. In Eritrea, water supply is grossly inadequate, especially in rural areas. There 
is a heavy burden on women and girls particularly during the dry season, when they spend a great deal 
of their time and energy fetching water from distant sources. The water and sewage systems,
especially in urban centers, are obsolete.
48. Increased urbanization has added a strain on shelter provision. Alternative building materials,
affordable by all, are not adequately available and access to land is a constraint to housing
development.
49. Eritrea is taking measures to increase access to safe water and adequate sanitation, establish
sustainable management systems, implement the Eritrean Rural Water Supply and Environmental
Sanitation programme (ERIWESP), establish an inventory of water points, standardize water lifting
equipment and civil structures for the water system, and to develop capacity at all levels. It is also
promoting construction of low cost housing to meet the needs of an expanding population.
50. Environment and Energy: International goals embodied in Agenda 21 include the integration of 
environmental protection in development planning, sustainable management of dry land, the reduction 
of green house gases and the conservation of biodiversity. 
51. Eritrea has ratified three international environmental conventions relating to Desertification,
Biodiversity and Climate Change, and is now working towards their implementation. In 1995 the
National Environmental Management Plan of Eritrea (NEMP-E) was prepared through an extensive
consultation with stakeholders. Guidelines for Environmental Impact Assessment were issued in
1999. A National Environmental Law is under preparation, and the development of a national
environmental information system envisaged. Since 1992 the Government has embarked on an
intensive programme of soil and water conservation with significant achievements. The MoA has
recently initiated an integrated watershed management programme that addresses erosion control in a 
comprehensive way.12

52. Recovery (Rehabilitation, Reintegration and Reconstruction): Peaceful conflict resolution and
lasting peace and security are among the international community’s prime goals. International
conferences have also focused on preparedness, prevention and response to natural and human made 
disaster, including food emergencies, the adoption of integrated policies to address them and the
promotion of a community based approaches to vulnerability reduction. 
53. Eritrea finds itself in a state of emergency with enormous rehabilitation, reintegration and
reconstruction needs. Government objectives include the provision of emergency needs for the
drought affected population, internally displaced people (IDPs) and expellees, the repatriation and
reintegration of returning refugees, the demobilization of the armed forces, and the rehabilitation and 
reconstruction of war and drought affected areas. Emergency interventions, therefore, have to be
planned with rehabilitation and reconstruction requirements in mind.

66. To mobilize resources for its high
priority needs, the Government organized
a conference for its development partners
and the private sector in September 2001.
At this meeting it presented its
Transitional Economic Growth and
Poverty Reduction Strategy that lays out
government’s policies for macroeconomic

67. The Government has also indicated that as the next step it will produce an Interim Poverty
Reduction Strategy Paper (I-PRSP), that is planned for release in July 2003, and prepares a medium
term development programme and strategy covering 2003-2005. The formulation of the I-PRSP is
foreseen to consist of two steps. The first is to carry out a comprehensive poverty assessment to gain 
a clear understanding of the extent, depth, distribution and causes of poverty. The second is to
systematically conduct public consultations in all parts of the country to ensure that the strategy
reflects the inputs of diverse groups. 
68. Economic development and poverty reduction have been the central goals of the government’s
development programme since independence. These goals are enshrined in the constitution in three
key clauses: 
The State shall work to bring about a balanced and sustainable development throughout the
country, and shall use all available means to enable all citizens to improve their livelihood in 
a sustainable manner, through their participation (Article 8, paragraph 2). 
Every citizen shall have the right of equal access to publicly funded social services. The State 
shall endeavor, within the limit of its resources, to make available to all citizens’ health,
education, cultural and other social services (Article 21, paragraph 1). 
The State shall secure, within available means, the social welfare of all citizens and
particularly those disadvantaged (Article 21, paragraph 2).
69. The government has pursued economic development and poverty reduction through a strategy
initially articulated in its Macro-Policy Paper of 1994 and more recently in its National Economic
Policy Framework and Programme presented in 1998. The strategy involves three main elements:
• Inducing widely-shared sustained economic growth by establishing a competitive environment
in which efficient, export-oriented private firms thrive; 17
UNDAF Eritrea, 2002 - 2006
• Raising the skills and well-being of people by investing in education, nutrition, health care, and 
water and sanitation systems;
• Reducing rural poverty by investing in rural infrastructure, agriculture, management of
livestock and pastures, and development of fisheries. 
70. Prior to the border conflict with Ethiopia, much progress was made promoting growth and
increasing access to services and opportunities. Although progress has been disrupted because of the 
conflict, government remains committed to this development strategy and plans to continue
implementing it for the coming years. 
71. The Transitional Economic Growth and Poverty Reduction Strategy highlights the successes
that the government achieved, in the pre-conflict 1992-97 period, in providing basic social services,
rehabilitating and expanding physical infrastructure, streamlining the political and administrative
structures, as well as achieving sustained economic growth through effective macroeconomic
management and creating an enabling environment for private sector growth. These successes also
reflect the government’s commitment to move away decisively from the central planning system that 
it had inherited at independence.
72. The border conflict and subsequent war with Ethiopia coupled with a persistent drought during 
1998-2000 have, unfortunately, seriously disrupted this promising growth. The prolonged conflict has 
also had devastating human and social impacts. The deportation from Ethiopia of Eritreans and
Ethiopians of Eritrean origin, dislocation of families from affected border areas, and the disruption of 
normal family lives due to the mobilization of men and women for national defense have created a
heavy social burden and humanitarian crisis. 
73. The adverse economic impact has included not only a serious deterioration in macroeconomic
performance over the 1998-2000 period, but also the damage caused to the economy has been
enormous. Direct war damage to roads and bridges, power and telecommunications installations,
schools, clinics, water supply and sanitation facilities, houses, factories, businesses and farms is
estimated to total over US $565 million, approximately 100 percent of 1999 GDP. Drought,
displacement of farmers and removal of land from cultivation because of landmines collectively
reduced agricultural output by 62 percent in 2000. Grain output in the country fell from a total of
460,000 metric tons in 1998 to 85,000 metric tons in 2000. During the coming 12-18 months, nearly 
half of Eritrea’s population will require food assistance. Port revenues, that constituted 20 percent of 
government revenues during 1995-97, declined by about two-thirds due to Ethiopia’s unilateral
decision not to use Eritrean ports for transshipment trade. During 1998–2000 they represented only
about 4 percent of government revenues. Uncertainty arising from the war, a decline in aggregate
demand, and a shortage of manpower led to sharp declines in private sector activity. Exports of food 
and livestock, beverages, salt, other commodities, manufactured goods, machinery and transport
equipment have also declined sharply. 
74. The Transitional Economic Development and Poverty Reduction Strategy of September 2001
has identified its development assistance priorities in terms of two distinct time frames. The
government’s immediate priorities, covering 2001-02, are to rebuild the economy, restore social
services and complete the economic and political reforms initiated before the conflict began. For the
medium term, 2003-05, government’s overarching objectives are to attain rapid, sustainable, widely18

shared economic growth and reduction of poverty in an environmentally sound manner, led by a
dynamic private sector.
75. Specifically, the government’s priorities over the next two years or so are to focus on: 
• Meeting immediate needs for emergency humanitarian assistance: During 2001 and 2002, Eritrea 
will require a minimum of 200,000 metric tons of food assistance to avoid a famine and 435,000
metric tons to meet the country’s basic food requirements. Donors have already pledged a total of
302,000 metric tons for 2001. Government is seeking donor assistance to fill the remaining gap. 
• Reconstructing infrastructure and assisting displaced people resume their economic activities: 
Direct war damage to infrastructure and displacement of people in the country’s most productive
farming regions severely disrupted agricultural production during 2000. Government’s priority is to 
reconstruct damaged roads, bridges, irrigation and other infrastructure as quickly as possible to
enable farmers to obtain the inputs they need to cultivate their crops and ship them to market. It is 
also critical to reconstruct power and water supply systems, health clinics and schools, and to assist 
war-affected people, many of whom have lost their homes and all their possessions, to rebuild their 
lives.
• Restoring a stable and supportive fiscal and macroeconomic framework: Government’s priority is 
to bring fiscal, monetary and balance of payments positions back into balance to restore investor
confidence and reinvigorating economic growth. Government has already begun to take important
steps towards this end. It will, however, need balance of payments support to help finance critical
imports. The government has been working with the IMF to assess recent developments and explore 
policy options. Looking forward, the government plans to improve tax and customs policy and
administration, remove obstacles blocking access to land, improve financial services, and strengthen 
the investment center.
• Demobilizing and reintegrating combatants: Demobilizing soldiers and reintegrating them into the 
economy is another key step towards restoring macroeconomic and fiscal balance and
reinvigorating the economy. With the deployment of the UNMEE peacekeeping force, the
government is in the process of demobilizing soldiers. This will have a negative short-term impact 
on the budget, as the government will need to provide former soldiers with financial assistance to
cover basic needs and help them to reintegrate socially and economically. However, these are
short-term expenses, and in the longer term cutting military expenditures will have a positive impact 
on the budget. Multilateral and bilateral partners are providing grant and credit financing to help
with the short-term costs of demobilization.
• Reintegrating returning refugees: With the help of UNHCR and other partners, including the UN 
System, the Government is in the process of repatriating and reintegrating up to 180,000 Eritrean
refugees returning mainly from Sudan. For many returnees the programme also includes
resettlement in new areas involving the distribution of farming land. Provision of shelter, water
supply, health and education is at the center of the reintegration component of the programme.
Since the start of this new repatriation programme in 2001, over 41,000 have returned by the end of 
March 2002. The plan targets repatriating additional 60,000 in the remaining months of 2002, and a 
similar number in 2003.19

• Continuing previously initiated critical development projects: There are many essential on-going 
projects in the areas of power generation, water supply improvement, highways, airports and
telecommunications development, health and education, port rehabilitation and expansion, and
management of natural resources and the environment. Work on these projects must continue to
ensure that what has already been accomplished will not be lost due to neglect.
76. Over the medium term, 2003-05, the government’s development priorities include:
• Developing new export markets. 
• Rebuilding the port business.
• Increasing agricultural productivity. 
• Achieving macroeconomic stability. 
• Attracting private sector investment. 
• Privatizing government-owned enterprises.
• Developing a sound financial system. 
77. For the longer-term, the Transitional Economic Growth and Poverty Reduction Strategy
recognizes that building a strong economy will require overcoming a shortage of skilled manpower,
investing in infrastructure, raising institutional and administrative capabilities of both the public and
private sectors, and maintaining sound and flexible economic policies and government regulations. 
78. The Strategy document also presents a detailed discussion on developments and the way
forward in the areas of macroeconomic framework, economic services, and human development. The 
macroeconomic framework covers fiscal and monetary policy issues, financial sector policy, trade
policy and balance of payments, and investment policy. The section on economic services deals with 
issues in agriculture, forestry and fisheries; manufacturing; energy and mining; tourism; and
infrastructure. The section on human development covers education; health; early childhood

provides a time frame for activities. This matrix is presented as Annex II.
79. The strategy document has identified three areas of special emphasis in Eritrea’s current
economic development programme, which are also referred to as cross-sectoral priorities. These three 
areas are:
• Demobilizing and reintegrating soldiers.
• Enhancing the status and increasing the participation of women in development.
• Restoring, enhancing, and preserving Eritrea’s ecological integrity.
The strategy emphasizes that Eritrea’s development will depend on real and measurable progress
made in each of these areas.20

4.3 IMMEDIATE HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE 
89. The UN agencies that have development-oriented mandates operate on multi-year budgeting
frameworks and have well defined multi-year country programmes. On the other hand,
relief/humanitarian assistance from some UN agencies in natural or human-made disaster situations
generally calls for operations based on annual budgeting cycles because of the unforeseen nature and 
scope of the assistance that may be required. As a result, the resources required for supporting UN
programmes to deliver relief/humanitarian assistance are mobilized through special appeal processes 
on an annual basis.
90. The Consolidated Appeal Process (CAP) was mandated through General Assembly Resolution
46/182 (December 1991) which directed that “For emergencies requiring a coordinated response, the 
Secretary-General should ensure that an initial consolidated appeal covering all concerned
organizations of the system, prepared in consultation with the affected state, is issued…”. The CAP is, 
firstly, a strategic planning tool and, secondly, a fundraising tool, which is predicated on humanitarian 
principles and human rights; complementarities among humanitarian partners; and capacities and
vulnerability analysis. The main steps of the CAP comprise (a) an inter-agency assessment and
analysis of the humanitarian emergency; (b) development of a coherent strategy as to how to respond; 
(c) implementation of the interventions (programmes) by the various agencies; and (d) monitoring and 
evaluation of the programmes.22

4.4 ASSISTANCE PROGRAMME OF THE WORLD BANK
94. The World Bank is a major partner in the reconstruction and development of Eritrea, with
several of its support projects and activities having linkages with ongoing or planned UN System
assistance programmes. In addition to elaborating these complementary linkages, a brief description 
of the Bank’s current programme of assistance helps in defining the broader development setting, and 
particularly the ODA situation, within which the UNDAF is conceived and will be implemented.
95. The World Bank portfolio consists of a number of projects covering infrastructure development 
and rehabilitation, health, human resources development, demobilization and reintegration of
combatants and early childhood development. Two major programmes initiated in the aftermath of the 
recent border conflict with Ethiopia are the “Emergency Reconstruction Programme” (ERP), and the
“Demobilization and Reintegration Programme” (DRP), the latter being actively supported by the UN 
system. While the ERP, also supported by a number of bilateral donors, made it possible for the Bank 
to respond quickly to the Government’s request for urgent assistance in repairing the widespread
damage caused by the war, the similarly multi-donor DRP, yet to be launched, is also critical to
macro-economic stabilization, reconstruction and economic recovery by virtue of its direct impact on 
reducing Government defense expenditure to levels that the country can afford.
96. Other ongoing programmes include a project to combat HIV/AIDS, Malaria, STDs and
Tuberculosis (HAMSET), an Integrated Early Childhood Development project, and a Cultural Assets 
Rehabilitation project. Implementation of two earlier projects, Ports Rehabilitation and Human
Resources Development, was severely affected by the war, though progress has been satisfactory 
following the peace agreement.
97. The Bank’s new lending programme is anchored in the above-mentioned demobilization
programme and continued support for basic infrastructure through community development. It
envisages that good progress on demobilization, governance and macro-economic stabilization would 
trigger further support in education, roads and power. The envisaged Roads Sector Development
Programme aims at improving road access in the most agriculturally productive parts of the country,
while the main objective of the Power Distribution Project is to rehabilitate the power distribution
system in and around Asmara, which accounts for the bulk of activity in the industrial sector. An
Education, Technical and Vocational Training project will begin to tackle one of the major
weaknesses of the Eritrean economy – a high adult literacy rate coupled with very low elementary and 
secondary enrolment rates and poor learning outcomes. Importantly, it will also support the
reintegration of demobilized soldiers into the economy through technical and vocational training.
98. The new lending programme will also support the Community Development Programme (CDP) 
that will succeed the highly rated Eritrea Community Development Fund (ECDF). It will continue
support for the building of economic and social service infrastructure in rural areas, as well as the
Village Bank Savings and Credit Scheme. This component of the CDP will complement the
demobilization programme, as it would provide micro-credit for demobilized soldiers to start or
rebuild small enterprises.24

4.5 STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES OF UN DEVELOPMENT SUPPORT
99. The goal of the UN country team in Eritrea is to contribute towards fostering peace and good
governance, achievement of post-conflict recovery and strengthening basic social services, building
sustainable livelihoods and equitable economic growth to promote the achievement of the overarching 
goal of poverty reduction. The UN Country Team in Eritrea, in close consultation with the
Government and key stakeholders, has agreed upon three key strategic objectives for UN System
support under the first UNDAF for Eritrea:
ß Promotion of Democratic Governance.
ß Promotion of Access to Quality Basic Social Services.
ß Promotion of Pro-Poor Economic Growth and Sustainable Livelihoods. 
100. To promote democratic governance, the UN system in Eritrea will support: the development of 
a justice system that fosters the rule of law and social justice; the development and strengthening of 
participatory decentralized institutions; development of an effective, efficient, transparent and
accountable civil service; facilitate the participation of civil society organizations in national
development processes; and advocate the ratification of global conventions.
101. To promote access to basic quality social services, the UN system agencies will support: the
development of an education and training system that can meet the national needs and the global goal 
of equitable quality primary education for all by 2015; work towards improving the nutritional status 
of the population, especially women and children; support government programme on early
childhood development, and initiatives aimed at ensuring that all individuals and families have access 
to fully integrated quality health services, including reproductive and sexual health, through
governmental and non-governmental facilities and community health services; and support
government efforts to provide all citizens with access to shelter, safe and adequate water, sanitation
and a hygienic environment. 
102. To promote pro-poor economic growth and sustainable livelihoods, the UN system’s assistance 
will be focused on providing: support for government initiatives and programmes to achieve pro-poor 
economic growth; reducing food insecurity to alleviate poverty; support for sustainable management 
of the environment, natural resources and energy; expanded access to telecommunications and
internet services; and support for the collection, analysis, and dissemination of data needed for
development planning, including a comprehensive poverty assessment. 
103. Halting and beginning to reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS is one of the millennium goals for
international development assistance (United Nations Millennium Declaration, September 2000).
Furthermore, in June 2001, the United Nations General Assembly Special Session on HIV/AIDS has
recognized that HIV/AIDS is a global emergency and one of the most formidable challenges to human 
life and dignity. At present, Eritrea is in a fortunate position of having a low prevalence and a strong 
political commitment to controlling this epidemic. The government is implementing a major
“HIV/AIDS, Malaria, STDs, Tuberculosis (HAMSET) Control Project” that is being financed through 
a 40 million dollar loan from the World Bank’s IDA credit facility. Under the first UNDAF for
Eritrea, the UN system agencies will support the promotion of a strong multi-sectoral national
response to HIV/AIDS and other key diseases.25

4.6.5 Supporting an Expanded National Response to HIV/AIDS
131. An expanding national response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic will require a coordinated thrust in 
the following areas: prevention of the further transmission of HIV, especially in the context of a
conflict and disaster affected country; provision of care, support and treatment to affected individuals, 
families and communities, especially to children orphaned and made vulnerable by HIV/AIDS;
alleviation of the social and economic impact of HIV/AIDS; strengthening of leadership and
multisectoral programming; and protection of the human rights of affected populations. The
objectives and strategies of the UN system support in these areas are outlined below.
132. Prevention of HIV transmission: The objectives of the UN system’s assistance include: (i) to
increase access of young people aged 15-24 to information through peers, educators and media and to 
the means to prevent and control HIV/AIDS; (ii) to reduce HIV infection rates in young people aged 
15-24 years by at least 25 percent by 2005; (iii) to ensure that all health workers know and practice 
blood safety procedures and universal precautions at all health facilities; (iv) to prevent mother-tochild transmission of HIV by 20 per cent by 2005; (v) to reduce the number of infants infected with
HIV by 15 per cent, by increasing the screening and provision of voluntary counseling and testing at 
antenatal care in all health services; (vi) to develop workplace-based prevention and care programmes 
among the public sector and civil society, including the private sector; (vii) to address the needs of
those most vulnerable to, and at greatest risk of HIV infection; (vii) to ensure technical and advisory 
support for the implementation of a comprehensive HIV/AIDS programme in the peacekeeping
mission; and (viii) to expand services for UN Staff and their families. The strategies to implement
these objectives include: (i) supporting the implementation of the national behavior change and
communication strategy; (ii) condom programming to improve access to and use of condoms; (iii)
training of health staff on blood safety procedures; (iv) promoting access of children and adolescents 
in and out of school to information, life skills, services, care and support and preventing new
infections through bolder action to ensure that all children, adolescents and caregivers are fully
informed about HIV/AIDS; (v) promoting safe sexual behavior among young people; (vi) minimizing 
mother-to-child transmission of HIV and developing a related policy on infant and young child
feeding practices; (vii) establishing workplace-based prevention, care and support programmes in key 
national economic and social sectors, and in the private sector; (viii) accelerating prevention activities 
and developing care and support programmes in the Eritrean Defense Force (EDF); (ix) minimizing
the risks of HIV transmission linked to demobilization; (x) minimizing the risks of HIV transmission 
linked to post-conflict movements of population, including returnees, IDPs, population returning to
the Temporary Security Zone (TSZ), etc.; (xi) supporting the implementation of a comprehensive
HIV/AIDS Programme for all UNMEE peacekeeping personnel; (xii) expanding the “Caring for Us” 
Programme of the UN Theme Group on HIV/AIDS (UN TG).
133. Care, Support and Treatment: The objectives of the UN system’s assistance include: (i) to
provide care and support to individuals, households and communities affected by HIV/AIDS; (ii) to
train health staff on in-patient care and support; (iii) to provide access to education, health and social 
services for orphans and children in families affected by HIV/AIDS. The strategies to implement
these objectives include: (i) increasing the quality and coverage of care and support across the
continuum for people infected and affected by HIV/AIDS; (ii) expanding voluntary counseling and
testing services (VCT); (iii) providing technical assistance for the training of health staff on clinical
care and counseling; (iv) developing a strategic plan to improve access to essential drugs for common 
and opportunistic HIV/AIDS-related diseases, an then to antiretroviral therapy; (v) building capacity35
UNDAF Eritrea, 2002 - 2006
for the development of community and home based care and support programmes; (vi) strengthening 
health and education services, and family and community networks to provide care and support for
children, adolescent and parents with HIV/AIDS.
134. Alleviation of Social and Economic Impact and Strengthening Leadership and Multi-sectoral 
Programming: The objectives of the UN system’s assistance include: (i) to support the development 
of policies, legislation and programmes which address individual and societal vulnerability to
HIV/AIDS and lessen its socioeconomic impacts, (ii) to provide policy guidance on the difficult
challenge of integrating HIV/AIDS priorities into the core of development planning, domestic
resource allocation processes, and sectoral plans; (iii) to ensure an extraordinary response to the
epidemic, including full engagement of top-levels leaders, measurable goals and targets, effective
policies and programmes supported by improved epidemiological and strategic information, adequate 
and sustained financial resources, and integration of HIV/AIDS prevention and care strategies into the 
mainstream planning and development efforts; (iv) to promote the full participation of people living
with and affected by HIV/AIDS in the response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic. The strategies to
implement these objectives include: (i) formulating and implementing a Poverty Reduction Policy and 
Strategy that takes into account the socioeconomic impact of HIV/AIDS; (ii) mainstreaming of
HIV/AIDS into core assistance programmes of all agencies; (iii) strengthening national capacity for
the development and implementation of integrated and multi-sectoral HIV/AIDS programmes; (iv)
revising and updating the 5-Year National Strategic Plan on HIV/AIDS; (iv) promoting the greater
involvement of individuals living with or affected by HIV and AIDS (GIPA).
135. Protection of the Human Rights of Affected Populations: The objectives of the UN system’s
assistance include: (i) to promote a human rights approach that includes the formulation of antidiscrimination laws; and (ii) to support innovative activities that addresses the role of power
imbalances between women and men and the role of gender relations in HIV transmission, including 
the impact of HIV/AIDS on women infected and affected, the added burdens of caring imposed on
women and girls, and inequality in access to prevention, treatment, care and support. The strategies to 
implement these objectives include: (i) developing, reviewing and reforming, as appropriate, public
health and other legislation, with the view of addressing HIV/AIDS in a non-discriminatory manner; 
(ii) assisting the Government to develop anti-discrimination practices and laws that protect vulnerable 
people, including those living with HIV/AIDS and with disabilities, from discrimination; and (iii)
mainstreaming gender into HIV/AIDS programmes.36
