4.7 COOPERATION STRATEGIES
136. In the implementation of the UNDAF, UN Agencies will, as a matter of priority, and where
there is clear added value, carry out joint programmes. This will involve undertaking joint
assessments of problems as required, and designing interventions consisting of shared objectives,
strategies, actions, timeframes,
resource requirements and clear
delineation of responsibilities.
137. Based on assessments to be
carried out by the Thematic Groups
and Sub-groups (see para. 142), the
UN Country Team will identify,
within three to six months of
launching the UNDAF, areas in the
UNDAF that are amenable to joint
programming, encompassing two or
more agencies, and those which, by
their technical nature or special donor 
requirements, would best be
implemented through parallel or
individual programmes or projects. It
will subsequently embark on
developing joint or parallel
programmes in the areas identified, a
process that would involve the
designation of a lead UN agency for
each joint or parallel programme. This 
designation would be based on criteria 
such as mandate, country presence,
relationship with the Government, comparative advantage and expertise, resources it is putting at the 
disposal of the joint programme and its present capacity to implement and comply with financial,
audit and reporting requirements.
138. These joint/parallel programmes would be based on national programmes in the respective
sectors. Where national programmes do not exist, the UN system is committed to assisting the
Government in their formulation as a matter of priority.
139. In the process of formulating detailed programme documents each agency will pay special
attention to such cross-cutting issues as gender, capacity development, equity, and population groups 
with special needs. In the formulation of the programmes, in addition to incorporating cross-cutting 
themes, it will be ensured that: (i) the planned programme delivery mechanisms are based on a
participatory decentralized development strategy of the government that focuses on building the
capacity of communities to identify their high priority needs and empowers them to manage the
implementation of development activities in their communities; and (ii) given uncertainties about the 
level of resources that could be potentially available, the programme formulation process will also
adopt a flexible approach allowing for adjustments in programme activities in response to evolving
government priorities through a clearly identified process.37

142. The UNDAF is a framework that will
guide contributions of the UN system to the
development of Eritrea over a period of five 
years (2002-2006). Provisions for follow-up 
and review are necessarily based on the
principle that the socio-economic 
development and political context in which
the UNDAF is required to operate will
continue to evolve. The UNDAF, therefore,
will be reviewed annually and, if necessary
reoriented, to better respond to the needs of
the country.
143. In Eritrea, the programming cycles of UNDP, UNFPA, and UNICEF are fully harmonized with 
the UNDAF timeframe. Other UN agencies are guided by annual (e.g. UNHCR and WFP) and biannual (e.g. WHO and UNESCO) country programmes and associated budgeting cycles.
Notwithstanding these differences, the UNDAF will serve as the umbrella for the country cooperation 
frameworks and country programmes of all UN agencies over the next five years. The selection of
goals, objectives and strategies of the programmes of each agency will be fully consistent with the
UNDAF and each agency’s country programme will specify how they contribute to the achievement 
of UNDAF objectives and cooperation strategies.
144. The existing coordination mechanisms for UN system activities, to be further strengthened, will 
play an important role in ensuring effective monitoring and follow-up of the UNDAF implementation. 
They include:
The UN Resident Coordinator System (RCS): The Resident Coordinator System provides the
overall structure for coordination of the UN system’s humanitarian and development assistance in 
Eritrea. The UN Country Team (UNCT), composed of the heads of UN agencies present in the
country and headed by the RC, holds weekly meetings to discuss programme issues (both
development and humanitarian) as well as security and other issues of concern to the UN System.
Concurrent with the launching of UNDAF and the resulting need for enhanced coordination,
collaborative programming, follow-up and monitoring (incl. joint reviews), the UNCT has agreed 
to the strengthening of the Office of the Resident Coordinator. Hence, a UNCT Programme
Specialist as well as support staff will soon join the RC’s office.
The UNCT also oversees the work of an inter-agency committee that is responsible for the
operational/administrative side of UN System collaboration. The committee holds regular
meetings to ensure closer coordination in the management of the UN common premises and other 
operational issues. In addition, the annual Resident Coordinator Workplan serves as the main
instrument for UN System coordination at the operational level. 
Humanitarian Coordination: Due to the humanitarian emergency caused by the border crisis
with Ethiopia, and subsequent recovery and rehabilitation needs following the signing of the
Peace Agreement in December 2000, humanitarian coordination has assumed special urgency and 
prominence in the work of the UN System in Eritrea. The UN System is part of a wider41
UNDAF Eritrea, 2002 - 2006
humanitarian coordination structure in the country. Under the overall leadership of the
government, represented by the Eritrean Relief and Refugee Commission (ERREC), activities of
the various humanitarian players in Eritrea are coordinated in the framework of a humanitarian
coordination forum that holds monthly meetings. Under this forum, five sectoral working groups10
monitor the humanitarian situation and harmonise activities in their respective sectors, namely:
food aid and food security, shelter and household items, water and sanitation, health, and
education. In addition to meetings of the main sectoral working groups in Asmara, inter-agency 
coordination meetings are also held at the zonal level in three of the affected zones, i.e. GashBarka, Debub and Northern Red Sea.
The UN System plays a prominent role in the above-mentioned coordination forums. The
Resident Coordinator, who is also the UN Humanitarian Coordinator, is the co-convener of the
monthly forum with the Government. Similarly, each of the sectoral working groups is co-chaired 
by a representative of a UN agency most active in the particular sector. In his humanitarian
coordination functions, the Resident/Humanitarian Coordinator (R/HC) is supported by the Office 
for the Coordination of Humanitarian affairs (OCHA).
Humanitarian response by the UN system is institutionalised in the Consolidated Appeal Process 
(CAP). An important element of the CAP is joint assessment by UN Agencies, Government and
NGOs of the humanitarian needs and a coordinated strategy for the delivery of humanitarian
assistance. If conditions change, additional joint assessments are undertaken to mobilize
resources. In the last three years, the Consolidated Appeal Process has been an important vehicle 
for mobilizing resources to meet the humanitarian needs of populations affected by war and
drought. 
The UNCT also recently took the initiative to establish an inter-agency working group on
recovery. This group, which will be expanded to include representatives of Government and other 
partners, was necessitated by the evident need for coordination in the area of recovery
(rehabilitation, reconstruction, and reintegration) which is increasingly taking over from the 
emergency phase.
Humanitarian coordination and information sharing is greatly facilitated by the existence of the
Information and Coordination Centre (ICC), housed in ERREC and managed by OCHA. The
ICC, which operates under the joint auspices of ERREC and the UN R/HC, was established with 
financial support from UN agencies and NGOs. It plays a key role in humanitarian information
gathering and dissemination, facilitating the monitoring and updating of the humanitarian
situation and thereby enabling the humanitarian community to better respond to emerging needs. 
To enhance its role as the main centre for humanitarian data coordination and analysis, the ICC
was expanded in 2001 to include a Geographic Information System (GIS) unit.
145. Building on existing coordination mechanisms, particularly those established in the CCA
process, the following structures will be used for the coordination, monitoring and review of UNDAF 
implementation:

UNDAF Steering Committee: The existing UNDAF Steering Committee, consisting of UN
Heads of Agencies, Macro Policy and the Ministry of Local Government, will be maintained to
provide policy level oversight to the implementation, monitoring and review of the UNDAF. The 
expanded version of the Steering Committee will include, in addition to the above, Government
and UN co-chairs of the Thematic Groups and Sub-groups. Terms of reference of Steering
Committee as well as that of the Thematic Groups is given in Annex V.
Thematic Groups: To bring greater coherence to UN agencies’ programmes, a number of theme 
groups and sub-groups will be established. These groups will be responsible for: (a) ensuring that 
inter-agency joint programming opportunities are maximized; (b) coordination of UN agencies
programme activities in the focus area of the theme group; (c) coordination between UN system
agencies and relevant government ministries/agencies; and (d) joint monitoring, reviews and
evaluations of activities. Four theme groups, and six sub-groups will continue to provide themefocused follow up to UNDAF implementation11. These are: I. Basic Social Services, under which 
there are four sub-groups, namely: (i) Health and Nutrition (ii) Education (iii) Water and
Sanitation, and (iv) HIV/AIDS; II. Sustainable Livelihoods and Pro-poor Economic Growth, 
with (i) Poverty Reduction (ii) Food Security as sub-groups; III. Recovery; and IV. Data for
Development. Detailed description of these groups is provided in Annex IV-b. 
Common Database for Monitoring UNDAF Implementation: An on-line computerized
database will be developed to maintain up-to-date statistics related to the indicators for
monitoring UNDAF implementation as specified in Annex VI. The National Statistics and
Evaluation Office (NSEO) will have the primary responsibility for maintaining this on-line 
system with support from the UN Resident Coordination Office. It will be supported by
designated staff in the relevant Government and UN agencies who will be responsible for
updating parts of the system relevant to their mandates.
146. In addition to reviews of joint/parallel programmes, joint reviews will be pursued in as many
areas as possible. The strategy for monitoring and annual and mid-term reviews of progress on
achieving the objectives of the UNDAF recognizes that each UN agency has specific reporting
requirements on the monitoring and reviews of their programmes to their headquarters and/or
governing bodies. This will not only minimize the burden on the Government by reducing the number 
of programme review sessions, but would also increase coordination between UN system agencies as 
well as between the various ministries and agencies of the Government.
147. The joint monitoring/review process of UNDAF has minimal implications for each agency’s
programme review/evaluation activities that have many agency-specific uses. It will, however, entail a 
new task of consolidating agency reviews/evaluations for the joint review process in addition to
closely examining/reviewing, as a new element, issues of duplication, joint programming
opportunities/practices, and operational efficiency.

Thematic groups and their sub-groups will work to ensure that (a) inter-agency joint programming 
opportunities are maximized; (b) coordination of UN agencies programme activities in the focus area
of the theme group; (c) coordination between UN system agencies and relevant government 
ministries/agencies; and (d) joint monitoring, reviews and evaluations of activities. They will 
specifically undertake the following tasks:
Terms of Reference
• Monitor implementation of integrated thematic work plans including review of previous quarter

committee

prepare policy option appraisals for decision by steering committee
